tn.quote: Paleni has three tone levels: H[igh], M[id], and L[ow]. There is no clear evidence in Paleni for two or more structurally distinct M tones. Most syllables are level-toned, but there are some contour-toned <HL>, <LH>, <MH> and <LM> syllables. Syllables can be long or short. Many contour-toned syllables are long (bimoraic), either Cvv or CvL with a sonorant coda. However, Cv̀ and Cv̄ verbs may have Ipfv stems Cv̌ and Cv᷇, since the Ipfv stem always ends with an H-tone. Thus pà ‘come.Pfv’, but pǎ ‘come.Ipfv’, and kú ‘die.Pfv’ but kpa᷇ ‘die.Ipfv’.

tn.note: Three level tones H/M/L; contours (HL, LH, MH, LM, rare LHL) are tone sequences on one syllable, often from Ipfv final-H ablaut or contraction. corr.words: 3.6.4 Downstep and downdrift. Phonetic downstep can occur when a <HL> or <HM> syllable is followed by an H-tone. The gradual lowering of H-toned peaks over the course of a long prosodic phrase is downdrift. It is not indicated in transcription and is not clearly phonologized.

4511.prule: No Paluan-specific stress statement anywhere in the source. Space-stripped search of the whole book (stage C, 334 pp.) finds 'stress' only in the front matter and ch.1-2 (Timugon, pp.5-27), once in ch.6 (p.169, 'free, stressed pronouns') and once in ch.10 (p.292, the Sumambuq/Lees critique); 'accent' nowhere; the Paluan outline 10.3.1 (pp.286-291) and the Highland Murut preamble 10.3 (p.286, shared features a-d, all segmental or morphological) have no hit for stress, accent, penult, prosod-, pitch or tone, and every Paluan form is phonemic and unmarked (Prentice marks stress only inside phonetic brackets, p.14). The p.274 convention does not fill the gap: 'attention is focused mainly on those features which exhibit differences with Timugon', and the outline phonology section is scoped to 'an inventory of phonemes and a description of any distributional or allophonic features which differ significantly from the Timugon pattern', i.e. segmental matters; nothing on p.274 promises that a suprasegmental difference would be reported, so silence on Paluan stress is not evidence of sameness (B's point, confirmed against the page). The Timugon (Poros subdialect) rule, p.14, is non-phonemic strong stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (phonemic syllable = one vowel plus preceding consonant), quantity-insensitive, with initial weak stress when two or more syllables precede the strong stress. Penultimate stress for Paluan is therefore at most an inference from the monograph's structure, never a statement. Rutter 1929's headnote ('the accentuation, as in Malay, is on the penultimate syllable unless otherwise shown') is a blanket orthographic convention over thirteen Murut and Dusun wordlists by a non-linguist, with no accent marks in the Peluan column; consistent with the inference, not a Paluan description.

4512.dq: A word is bordered by word juncture (which is characterized by potential pause) and marked by primary stress on the ultima. Word juncture is represented by space.
4512.heavy: Primary stress is quantity-insensitive. Long vowels carry a length-linked secondary stress with a pitch rise ('Secondary stress accompanied by a rise in pitch occurs on long vowels', p. 28); e and o are always long, a/i/u contrast short vs long (pp. 37-38).
4512.prule: Primary stress on the ultima (final syllable) of every word, regardless of syllable count or vowel length; realized as loudness on a low pitch ('a low push').
4512.srule: Secondary stress, accompanied by a rise in pitch, falls on every long vowel wherever it stands in the word (vowel length is contrastive for a, i, u; e and o are always long); placement is by vowel length, not by position or alternation, so a word without a long vowel has only the final primary stress. Loan vowels stressed in Spanish become long and carry this secondary stress (vaca > ba:ka, banco > ba:ngku).
4512.quote: A word is bordered by word juncture (which is characterized by potential pause) and marked by primary stress on the ultima. Word juncture is represented by space. Primary stress is characterized by volume, usually on the lowest pitch level of the speaker, but varying with the type of intonation contour. It is perhaps best described as a low push. Secondary stress accompanied by a rise in pitch occurs on long vowels. 4519.prule: Primary stress on the first (leftmost) long vowel in the word; if the word has no long vowel, on the first syllable. 4519.srule: Words whose primary stress is on a non-initial long vowel: secondary stress on the first syllable. Exception: the verbaliser -ma- is stressed and the following suffix is not (mirli-ma-larta 1-3, karrara-ma-lku 1-4); -ma- never takes stress from a long vowel.

4522.dq: 例えば，休止により規定される多音節の音韻領域であれば，どのような統語単位であれ，同じような卓立（強さ）を観察することができる。… (5)(6)は語であり，(7)から(9)は句である。いずれも最終音節に卓立が現れるため，音調パターンによって単位を同定することは不可能である。 [Yamada 2011: 5] — one final-prominence rule for the pause-bounded domain, whether that domain is a word or a phrase; Yamada 2016: 12-13 applies the same 'fixed accent pattern (weak-strong)' to a compound word.
4522.dloc: Yamada 2011, §3 語と句の区別, journal pp. 5-6. Supporting: Yamada 2016, §2.1, pp. 12-13
4522.prule: Fixed final prominence: in every pause-delimited polysyllabic phonological domain, word or phrase alike, the last syllable is strong (●) and all preceding syllables weak (○): ○●, ○○●, ○○○●. Yamada 2016 calls this 'Parauk Wa's fixed accent pattern (weak-strong)' and derives minor (pre-)syllables from the weakening of the non-final syllable of a polysyllabic (compound) word. Word accent is not a distinctive (contrastive) feature. Weight plays no role in either statement.
4522.srule: None: one prominence per pause-delimited domain - '以下，音節を単位とする相対的な強さ・弱さをそれぞれ●，○と表す。… (6) ɲɛʔsioʔsiɔ（○○●）… (9) ruŋ krak yum kiʔ（○○○●）… いずれも最終音節に卓立が現れる' [relative strength written per syllable as ●/○: every non-final syllable weak, the final one strong, in 2-, 3- and 4-syllable domains]. (Silva 1999: 26) — the rule is stated for stems and words, with compounds treated stem by stem; no phrasal prominence is discussed.
4525.dloc: Silva 1999, cap. 2 'A fonologia', seção 2.1.3 'O acento', p. 26. Silva 2003, seção 4.1.5 'O acento', p. 42.
4525.prule: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the stem (tema), including stems extended by certain derivational suffixes; inflectional suffixes (e.g. argumentative case -a) never carry stress, so an inflected word surfaces with penultimate or antepenultimate stress while an uninflected stem is oxytone. Position is fixed by morphological structure (stem edge vs. inflectional suffix), not by a syllable count from the word edge and not by weight.
4525.srule: Only in compounds and derived stems: each stem (tema) of a compound is stressed (Silva 1999: 26 'Nas composições, cada tema é acentuado'); compound or derived stems 'podem ter acentos primários e secundários', the primary on the last syllable of the final stem or derivational suffix and the secondaries on the preceding stems, e.g. wyráxíga 'garça', awaxí'ía 'arroz', morópiaréra 'assassino', oxokáwa'é 'o que mata', onopónopó '3 bater muito' (Silva 2003: 42). No rhythmic secondary stress is described for simple words.

4526.dq: Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word.
4526.dloc: dos Santos 2024 §3.2.1 'Sound inventory, phonotactics and stress', p. 40 ('Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word').
4526.prule: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the lexical root ('Stress is assigned to the root-final syllable of a word'). The obligatory nominalizing enclitic =a on nouns is extrametrical, so nouns surface with penultimate stress ([ɲã.ˈndu.a] 'spider', [ta.pi.ˈʔi.ɾa] 'tapir') while bare verb forms surface with final stress ([ɛ.ˈpi], [ɛ.kɨ.ˈtʃi]); the negation circumfix nd(a)-...-i leaves stress on the root ([nd-aĩˈmbɛ-i]); a stated set of suffixes triggers stress shift off the root: -ahim 'very' and -uhu 'aug' are named in the prose, and exx. (15)-(16) are cited as 'evidence of stress shift due to suffixation in nouns', ex. (16) containing only the diminutive -ʔi (named as 'the diminutive suffix /-ʔi/' on the same page); the transcriptions show the shifted stress on the suffix ([aĩmbɛ-aˈhĩm], [j-ipi-uˈhu], [vɨɾaˈʔia]), which the prose does not state. Position is set by morphological structure (root edge plus affix identity), not by syllable count from a word edge and not by syllable weight. Marçoli 2018 states the same for Tenharim/Jiahui/Amondawa: 'o acento tônico deve ocorrer sempre na última sílaba da raiz, tornando-a palavra oxítona' (p. 122); 'O acento, nesta língua, é apenas demarcatório: ele marca sempre a última sílaba da raiz, mudando mais à direita apenas nos casos de derivação ou de composição quando o segundo termo também comporta tonicidade' (p. 77).
4526.srule: No rule stated. dos Santos 2024 (Juma/Jupaú) does not mention secondary stress and marks primary stress only (§3.2.1 pp. 40-41; 'I indicate primary stress... with the diacritic (ˈ)', §3.2.3.1 p. 42). Marçoli 2018 (Tenharim/Jiahui/Amondawa) lists 'ˌ acento silábico secundário' among his symbols and writes it in a few transcriptions without comment ([ɲãˌpɛkã'ndi] 'gavião' p. 79, [ajˌpinã'ŋga] 'pai' p. 106, [ipuˌtũnũ'hu] 'escuro' p. 121); his one statement: when a stressed suffix (-ete 'genuine', -uhu 'aug') or a second noun takes the main stress, 'em algumas composições, permite-se conservar o acento de cada palavra', the root keeping its final-syllable stress as secondary ([paˌkɔʋu'hu] 'banana nanica', [kũˌɲã'ŋgwɛɾɐ] 'mulherada', p. 123).

4528.tone: Voorhoeve 1975: 390 (own 1966-1974 fieldwork on the easternmost Ba dialect): 'There is some evidence that the language has contrastive pitch, possibly a high and a low tone.' Nothing on stress or accent. Suter & Usher 2017 (Language & Linguistics in Melanesia 35), the family survey, state flatly for all three Kamula-Elevala languages (p. 109) 'The languages are tonal, but the lexical data we have for them does not include a transcription of tone' and (p. 116) 'all three languages are tonal... The role stress played in the history of the Kamula-Elevala languages is not well understood'; for Pa specifically (p. 110) 'Voorhoeve (1975: 390) mentions that Pa has contrastive pitch, but tones are not represented in Waldeck's orthography'. Their tonal claim for Pa rests on Voorhoeve's sentence, not on new data. Usher's New Guinea World Pa page paraphrases it as 'suggested but not affirmed'. The stress remarks in Suter & Usher (contrastive stress, vowel loss under stress) concern Aekyom and Kamula, not Pa.

4529.dq: In Paresi, word stress has delimitative functions in that it indicates word boundaries. [...] I did not use data from lists of words in isolation because in words in isolation phrasal intonation may interact with stress. A phrasal intonation in Paresi is defined by Silva (2013: 108) as a raising in pitch at the end of a phrase and a lowering at the beginning of the next phrase.
4529.dloc: §2.5.1 'Stress patterns', pp. 55-61; quoted passage pp. 55-57; summary line p. 4 (§1.1 Linguistic profile); diphthong inventory §2.4.1 pp. 52-53; vowel lengthening §2.1.2.3 p. 28.
4529.heavy: 'a heavy syllable with two moras: CVV' (p. 57). CVV = diphthong: §2.4.1 (pp. 53-54) lists the diphthongs /oa/, /ae/, /oe/, /ai/, /ei/, /oi/, /ao/ and says 'all sequences are heavy syllable with two moras, which attract stress in a word'; glide-vowel [jV]/[wV] sequences are consonant+vowel, not diphthongs (§2.4.2). Vowel lengthening is 'marginally contrastive' (demonstratives, interjections, ideophones; §2.1.2.3 p. 28) and plays no role in the stress rule. Minimal word is bimoraic (p. 59: monosyllabic stems /'tʲoa/, /'ao(-ka)/ are heavy).
4529.dflt: penultimate syllable of the stress domain (root plus counted suffixes; proclitics, prefixes and the suffixes -ti, -ta, -nae, -ne, -re are excluded from the count)
4529.prule: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stress domain (root plus counted suffixes); a heavy CVV syllable (diphthong) attracts stress away from the penult, to the final (kotyói, irái, alatái, ferakóa) or the antepenult (káimare, wáinama). The same rule is stated in Brandão 2010 p. 11 for 'words with up to three syllables': 'i) if the last syllable is heavy and the penultimate syllable is light, stress the last syllable...; ii) in the absence of a heavy syllable, stress the penultimate syllable'. CAUTION: the 2010 passage continues 'In polysyllabic words with suffixes, the main stress falls on the final syllable (Brandão, 2009b)'; the 2014 grammar reverses that clause (suffixes -ti, -ta, -nae, -ne, -re are outside the count; 'Contrary to my analysis in which suffixes do not get stress', p. 56), so only clauses (i)-(ii) of the 2010 rule carry over.
4529.srule: Words with more than three syllables in the stress count (proclitics, prefixes and the suffixes -ti, -ta, -nae, -ne, -re excluded) take a secondary stress two syllables before the primary-stressed syllable ([ˌθe.ko.'ha.tse.ti] 'leader', [ˌka.he.'ha.li.ti] 'illness'), repeating leftward in longer words per the transcriptions in (81) ([ˌe.ha.ˌna.ne.'ha.re], [ma.ˌwai.ja.ˌka.la.'ha.re]); a heavy CVV syllable can take the secondary stress instead, the primary then shifting ([i.ˌdʲai.he'ne.re], (82)); shorter words carry only a primary stress (the source's 'less than three' / 'more than three' wording leaves the exactly-three case unstated). In bound-noun compounds the first noun's stressed syllable is secondary (§4.4 p. 178).
4529.quote: In Paresi, word stress has delimitative functions in that it indicates word boundaries. In general, stress occurs in the penultimate syllable of a word. Acoustically, vowel duration may be the main correlate of stress. [...] Paresi exhibits a penultimate stress pattern, as shown in (71), contrary to the analysis in Silva (2013) where stress is not predictable in monomorphemic words. There are few trisyllabic and polysyllabic noun stems (without any suffixes) and they also follow this pattern. [...] (71) a. toto ['to. to] 'breast' b. kafaka [ka.'fa.kɐ] 'yesterday' c. tihanare [ˌti.ha.'na.re] '…
4529.loc: §2.5.1 'Stress patterns', pp. 55-61; quoted passage pp. 55-57; summary line p. 4 (§1.1 Linguistic profile); diphthong inventory §2.4.1 pp. 52-53; vowel lengthening §2.1.2.3 p. 28.
4529.idn: the Paresi variety spoken by the people in the Rio Formoso area, 'the majority variety' (associated in the literature with the Kozarene group; the minority variety, associated with the Waimaré group and spoken in Bacaval village, is described by Silva 2009 and Drude 1995); data: Formoso, Cachoeirinha, JM and Rio…
4529.exq_: However, there are exceptions to this stress pattern. Some words receive stress on the last or antepenultimate syllable. This case can be explained by syllable weight. [...] Another exception to the penultimate stress pattern is when stress is the only feature marking meaningful contrast in a few p…
4529.tone: The grammar does not mention tone or pitch accent anywhere (no occurrence of 'tone'/'tonal'/'pitch accent' in the text); §2.5 Prosody treats only stress, so absence of tone is inferred from silence, not stated. Brandão attributes the word-final pitch rise heard in isolation forms to phrasal intonation (citing Silva 2013: 108), not to stress; vowel duration is the proposed main correlate of stress ('Acoustically, vowel duration may be the main correlate of stress').

4530.dq: Henning has adopted as a working hypothesis the principle of stress upon the final syllable within the word, which accords with later Western Iranian practice. The question of which words are to be stressed is often simplified by the fact that a poem with, apparently, three stresses to a line will contain many lines with only three words, or with three words and a conjunction or preposition.
4530.prule: No established rule. Word-final stress is only a working hypothesis (Henning's, adopted by Boyce for scanning the hymn-cycles, by analogy with later Western Iranian); Boyce says the position of stress in Middle Iranian is 'not yet certain' and Henning 1942 says it is 'impossible to say, with any degree of certainty, which syllable of a word bore the stress'. What the sources do assert: Parthian had a strong (intensity) stress, one stress per lexical word, with conjunctions, prepositions and enclitics unstressed (Boyce p. 53: a line-final unstressed syllable occurs only when a stressed word is followed by an enclitic).

PaTani has a word-tone pattern, where in polysyllabic morphemes only the first vowel has contrastive tone and subsequent syllable(s) have levelled tone, i.e. if the first syllable has a high tone, then subsequent vowels have slightly lower pitch; and if the first syllable has a low tone, then subsequent vowels have slightly mid pitch.

4536.prule: Tone language: every vowel (syllable) carries either high or low tone and may be oral or nasal; tone and nasalization are the only suprasegmental phonemes named. No stress rule is stated and the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the book.

4536.idn: Pawaian (no dialect named); data from the Walio clan; data: Walio clan of the Karimui Plateau (Eastern Highlands / Gulf Districts, then Territory of Papua and New Guinea); eighteen months of monolingual fieldwork by D. and J. Trefry; years not stated in the book (thesis 1965, published 1969)
4536.tone: Trefry 1969: 13 names nasalization and tone as Pawaian's two suprasegmental phonemes; every vowel carries high or low tone; lexical minimal sets are three-way at most (tone x nasalization). Note 3, p. 94: tone marks are omitted in the practical orthography unless the meaning is ambiguous. Stress/accent are never mentioned (my own check of with spaces stripped: 'stress' 0 hits, 'accent' 0, 'suprasegmental' 3, 'tone' 33). SIL OPD 2011 p. 3, under the heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', says only 'Tone is phonemic. Examples: sú [su] tooth, su [su] ginger, suú [su] road' and marks high tone with an acute only when needed. MacDonald 1973: 130-131, summarising Trefry, gives Pawaia 'A high-low tone system exists, and either tone may occur on all vowels'; its two uses of 'stress' (p. 117 on the name Kewa, p. 131 on Witu) do not concern Pawaia. No source denies stress explicitly, so the reading is 'tone system, stress unmentioned', not no word stress.
